title: Dividing a Decimal by a Whole Number

steps.body: Estimate a decimal quotient with nearby compatible values before dividing. The estimate checks whether the quotient's size makes sense.

invariants: A decimal is place value continued past the ones: computing in the smallest shared place turns g5dc div whole into whole-number arithmetic, and the point's position records which place the digits landed in.
misconceptions: Right-aligning digits instead of the points, treating a trailing zero as a change in value, or losing count of the decimal places a product carries.

options.label: Close to 0.36.
options.feedback: Correct — 1.44 shared four ways gives a little more than 0.3 per share.

options.label: Close to 4.
options.feedback: 4 is the number of shares, not the size of one — splitting 1.44 four ways must give pieces smaller than 1.44, and far smaller than 4.

options.label: Close to 0.04.
options.feedback: Four shares of 0.04 would rebuild only 0.16 — nowhere near 1.44. The share is ten times bigger; the decimal point slipped a place.

options.label: Close to 36.
options.feedback: A share cannot be larger than the whole being shared — 36 dwarfs 1.44. The digits 36 name 36 hundredths, an amount that sits below one half.

steps.body: Summarize dividing a decimal by a whole number.

concept.body: Think of 1.44 as 144 hundredths. Dividing 144 by 4 gives 36 hundredths, or 0.36.
concept.narration: Think of 1.44 as 144 hundredths. Dividing 144 by 4 gives 36 hundredths, or 0.36.

widget.prompt: Five equal shares are cut from 2.75. Read the whole as 275 hundredths, deal them out into the 5 shares, and count ONE share: how many hundredths does it hold?

commonErrors.feedback: 275 hundredths is the WHOLE being dealt out; the question asks what lands in just one of the 5 shares.
That subtracted the 5 instead of sharing by it — dealing into equal shares is division, not removal.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Deal the 275 hundredths into 5 equal piles, or find the number that times 5 makes 275.
